Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win Sign up for the Breaking News US email The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other , according to the New York Times. The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors. A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed. The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role. The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December . Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race. Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference. Continue reading...

stories.description: The Guardian’s UK politics blogger answered readers’ questions These are from my colleague Peter Walker , who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor. Peter posted this before the result was announced. Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport. Cleverly says he would “end Khan’s war on motorists”, which is a sign he might lean into the anti-cycling and walking rhetoric which the London Tories have a habit of espousing. Expect talk about LTNs and 20mph zones. In the media Q&A Cleverly is pinned down on whether he backs the Tory party line on wanting to leave the ECHR and opposes net zero. He confirms he does (as he has to). Such things will be ready ammunition for Labour. Cleverly says of Andy Burnham, “His residual behaviour is to be anti-London”. This will very much be a theme of his campaign, it seems. Not sure how resonant a “poor London!” message will be even in London People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related. The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. Continue reading...

stories.description: Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”. As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024 . A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip. Continue reading...

stories.description: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples. The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression against its territory, including the attack launched today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, by drones that were intercepted and destroyed by air defense systems in the Kingdom’s airspace. This comes two days after a similar attack at dawn on Friday, November 13, 2026, by two drones that were also intercepted. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression. stories.title: Airport chaos continues after US ground stop lifted – as it happened
stories.description: This blog is now closed. See our full reports: US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop affecting all air travel Chaos at US airports as flight stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt Sign up for the Breaking News US email We’re wrapping up this live coverage of the US ground stop and travel chaos that followed – it’s just passed 12.50am in Washington DC. Below’s a rundown on what happened, and you can read a full report here . Thanks for being with us. The Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, throwing airports into sudden chaos, after a communications failure at air traffic control centres. More than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed , with another 1,500 already cancelled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline ⁠schedules for days. It was the longest flight shutdown since the attacks of September 11 2001. The FAA lifted the ground stop later on Friday, with transportation secretary Sean Duffy saying US airspace reopened at 8.15pm ET (0115 GMT). But departures would ⁠resume gradually and it would take ​time for airlines to restore normal operations, he warned. “It’s going to be slow.” All US-bound departures from European airports are suspended until 5am UTC on Saturday , according to a notice published by the European traffic control agency, Eurocontrol. US airlines including American, United and Southwest began resuming flights on Friday night. “Thank you for your understanding as we work as quickly as possible to fully restore normal operations,” Delta said. Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and it was “operational right now”. The system was “incredibly old”, he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.” There was no indication from preliminary investigations that the communications stoppage was tied to a “nefarious attack” , homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said. Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new air traffic control system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50bn to modernize it. Continue reading...

stories.title: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – as it happened
stories.description: This blog is now closed On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy , a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it. She said: I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work. The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second. Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said: The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch. He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes. It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’ I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not least because you’ve got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job. Milburn admitted this meant the plans would not be “pain-free”. I’m not saying that any of this will be easy or that it will be pain-free because it won’t. You know, candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. He said he wanted the system to prioritise improving people’s life chances in the long term over easing their financial hardship in the short term. Actually for young people there’s a different debate that we’ve got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances. I think what the current system does, it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that’s the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around. He said, alongside the cuts to benefits he is proposing (see 11.56am ), he wanted to improve employment support for young people. We need to make sure people have the opportunities to get an apprenticeship, a job, a work placement, a pre-apprenticeship, a college place. The menu of opportunities has got to increase. They’ll have a personal adviser, they’ll be coached all the way through. The adviser will stick with them until they have found a job or an apprenticeship or college place. He also confirmed he wants to let young people do some work before they start losing benefits. They will get immediate access to support if that’s what they need, if that’s the thing that is holding them back from being in education or training. He admitted that offering better employment support and mental health support would mean his plans would initially cost money. According to the Times, he did not did not deny claims the whole package could cost £6bn. But, in the long run, there would be savings, he said. Obviously this costs money. And frankly it’s a better use of money, both from the point of view of the young person and the taxpayer, to spend that money getting them into work rather than spending that money keeping them on benefits. This is the sort of fatuous thing about this debate. You’ve got to invest upfront in order to get savings out of the back end. Cost-free is fatuous. So we’ve got to be candid about that. It will need significant investment. To get a return on investment will take time … the only way of cutting the benefits bill sustainably is by getting young people into work, paying their taxes and being less reliant on benefits. Unless you are prepared to put the investment upfront it will never be possible. He said he was “confident” that Andy Burnham was full-square behind the changes that are needed.” Continue reading...

Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic. The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. That has been exacerbated by successive governments ducking politically unpalatable decisions for decades. That has scattered responsibility for the sector across and outside government in a way that few would design from scratch. This report makes for sober reading of how adult social care and those who rely on it have been systematically failed. The fragmentation we see today is what happens when there is a total absence of political leadership to ensure the sector is well-funded and provides equitable access to care. stories.title: Is the US blue wave a turning point for Europe, too?
stories.description: Far-right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for Trump’s betrayal. But the midterms also showed that democracy can fight back • Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here “Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone. The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has been met with understandable relief in European capitals. In the short term however, the worst for Europe is not over. Trump didn’t need congressional approval, after all, to unleash a trade war on his supposed European allies, threaten to invade Greenland, try to stitch up Ukraine or go to war with Iran, an act that has inflated fuel and food prices disastrously. The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration. stories.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
stories.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

stories.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
stories.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear. Continue reading...

It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

stories.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
stories.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. stories.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
stories.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. They sketch out what could be lost A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids . That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm , citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon ; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew , and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie. stories.description: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe. stories.title: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites
stories.description: Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court . It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths. At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish. I began to wonder if my meds were making me hallucinate. Continue reading...

Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

stories.title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag
stories.description: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round !” It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones. Continue reading...

stories.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
stories.description: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer , as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing . But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material. stories.description: Marko Kricak, an Aleksandar Vucic loyalist, is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into a gangland murder. Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election defeat.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack
stories.description: Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous weekends.
stories.subject: Finance

stories.title: Ukraine: Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
stories.description: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russia struck energy infrastructure in at least four regions overnight. Meanwhile, a Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire for the Kherson region is set to end on Sunday evening. DW has more.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Ukraine news: Oleshky ceasefire ends as Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
stories.description: A US-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region ended on Sunday night with no violations reported. Elsewhere, however, Russia struck energy infrastructure in at least four other regions. DW has more.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Ukraine: Six-day localized ceasefire in Oleshky comes to end
stories.description: A US-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region ended on Sunday night with no violations reported. But Russian drones and missiles hit other regions in Ukraine.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union
stories.description: Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Germany news: Gen Z group calls for new protests
stories.description: The group behind German demonstrations this weekend has called for more protests to keep pressure on the government to act. Meanwhile, the IG Metall union has begun warning strikes after pay talks collapse. DW has more.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
stories.description: Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. But new developments in biotech and AI are a cause for concern. DW addresses some of the most important questions about their history, risks, and control.
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto
stories.description: Clashes broke out as officers again dispersed housing protesters from tent camps in Lisbon and Porto. Portuguese police have repeatedly cleared tent camps erected across both cities in recent weeks.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions
stories.description: Thousands are expected to take part in the Indian opposition's planned mega march in New Delhi over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
stories.description: Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Germany's search for a nuclear waste site
stories.description: Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion Binance crypto theft
stories.description: The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: Bulgarians vote in highly polarized presidential runoff overshadowed by Ukraine war
stories.description: Voters in Bulgaria are choosing between two candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and ties with Russia. The runoff comes after a record-low turnout in the first round.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Bulgaria exit polls: Incumbent Yotova predicted to win
stories.description: Incumbent President Iliana Yotova appears set to win Bulgaria's presidential election runoff. Exit polls put the more Russia-friendly candidate who favors dialogue with Moscow on just over 50% of the vote.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Bolivia declares emergency as El Nino intensifies, threatens severe weather
stories.description: President Rodrigo Paz warned of severe droughts and flooding as El Nino intensifies, with at least 78,000 families already affected by drought.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Trump grants visa to mother of Ghanaian boy killed in NYC — Mamdani
stories.description: Javits Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot in a neighborhood in the Bronx. He was 15 years old.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
stories.description: After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
stories.description: Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Gen Z protests sweep cities across Germany
stories.description: Young people in Germany have taken to the streets in some 34 cities, calling for greater political say and a more hopeful future. The protests come amid a wave of youth demonstrations across Europe. DW has more.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday
stories.description: Protests led by young people were largely peaceful through the day, but reports about looting and rioting in the evening, especially in Frankfurt, overshadowed the spirit of the demonstrations.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Ukraine news: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Kyiv-controlled territory
stories.description: After Melania Trump reportedly brokered a localized truce, residents of Ukraine's Oleshky managed to leave the occupied city. Meanwhile, Kyiv claimed a hit on a Russian rocket fuel plant. DW has more.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Germany news: Merkel calls for first female president
stories.description: Former Chancellor Angela Merkel says it's time to consider a woman as Germany's next president. Meanwhile, Berlin's Left Party is deciding whether to enter coalition talks. DW has more.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Massive Gen Z protests set to sweep cities across Germany
stories.description: Young people in Germany are taking to the streets in some 34 cities, calling for greater political say and a more hopeful future. The protests come amid a wave of youth demonstrations across Europe. DW has more.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
stories.description: A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
stories.description: What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.
stories.subject: Science

stories.title: India news: Tanker carrying 27 Indians attacked in Strait of Hormuz
stories.description: Two vessels carrying Indian crew members have been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days as Iran steps up attacks on shipping. DW has more.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: India news: Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate vote theft in parliament
stories.description: Home Minister Amit Shah has challenged Rahul Gandhi to debate electoral irregularity allegations in parliament, ahead of a major opposition rally against the election chief in Delhi.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
stories.description: The mandate of the UN peacekeeping force in Western Sahara will expire on October 31. The UN Security Council could not agree on a resolution to extend the mission.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
stories.description: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declined to comment on Russia's participation in the G20 summit in December, telling DW that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should travel to Russia if he wanted talks with Vladimir Putin.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
stories.description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the firing of top court President Bogdan Swieczkowski as a move to "restore the rule of law."
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Poland: Protesters, police clash amid top court standoff
stories.description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the suspension of top court President Bogdan Swieczkowski as a move to "restore the rule of law."
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
stories.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership."
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Ukraine: Oleshky residents evacuate war-ravaged city
stories.description: Under the local ceasefire, an aid convoy of 25 buses arrived with humanitarian aid and as transport for fleeing Oleshky residents. The Ukrainian city has been occupied by Russia since 2022 and faces food shortages.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
stories.description: There is currently more irregular migration between eastern Libya and Crete, Greece. It's raising questions as to what connects people smugglers with powerful militias in eastern Libya and then in turn, Europeans.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Tennessee woman Christa Pike describes pain after failed execution
stories.description: Christa Pike says she remains in constant pain a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee. Her lawyers want her death sentence reduced to life, while the state governor has ordered an investigation.
stories.subject: Finance

stories.title: What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile
stories.description: Siarhei Tsikhanouski criticizes the work of his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and her office. He also questions her legitimacy. What are the implications for Belarusian political forces in exile?
stories.subject: World

stories.title: US midterms: Pope Leo XIV casts vote by mail
stories.description: As a US citizen, Pope Leo XIV is eligible to vote in US elections and has made use of that right with a postal ballot ahead of Tuesday's midterms. The pontiff, a Chicago native, did not reveal who he voted for.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Binance crypto exchange suspends trades over North Korea-linked hack
stories.description: Crypto platform Binance has suspended trading following a suspected hack now linked to North Korea. The disruption has left users unable to trade on the cryptocurrency platform while the suspected breach is investigated.
stories.subject: Finance

stories.title: Germany news: Merz calls for Korean reunification at DMZ
stories.description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed hope for Korean reunification during a visit to the heavily fortified border. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier has held talks with China's Xi Jinping in Beijing. DW has more.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Germany news: Merz hopes for Korean reunification at DMZ
stories.description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed hope for Korean reunification during a visit to the heavily fortified border. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier has held talks with China's Xi Jinping in Beijing. DW has more.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Seoul fears being sidelined as US reaches out to North Korea
stories.description: With ties between South Korea and the Trump administration strained, the South Korean government worries that Donald Trump's pursuit of a diplomatic breakthrough with Kim Jong Un may come at Seoul's expense.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport
stories.description: Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Italy: Students and workers rally over living costs
stories.description: Students and workers have marched across Italy for more school funding and relief from rising living costs. The rallies follow weeks of school occupations and protests against higher military spending.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
stories.description: German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Russia: Critical newspaper 'Novaya Gazeta' to close
stories.description: "Novaya Gazeta," one of the last remaining independent, critical media outlets in Russia, has announced it is closing under pressure from state authorities. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, evacuations have begun in Oleshky.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Brazil's new anti-gang law: Can it curb organized crime?
stories.description: A tough stance against organized crime? One year after a massacre that left more than 130 people dead, a new law aims to crack down on drug cartels in Rio's favelas.
stories.subject: Health

stories.title: IIHF ordered to allow Russia back into world championships
stories.description: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to take part in international ice hockey tournaments. The IIHF had banned Russia following the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age
stories.description: On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' cannot live from their pensions.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Europe's youth set to join mass cost of living protests in 25 countries
stories.description: Youth protests are set to take place in more than 25 countries in Europe on Friday and over the weekend, coalition organisers said, as demostrators seek to increase pressure on governments over issues including soaring housing costs and deteriorating learning conditions with a show of cross-border solidarity.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: 🔴 Live: Deadly Russian attacks damage two bridges in Kyiv, mayor says
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: FIFA: Infantino, Tashima and Diallo enter presidential race
stories.description: Three candidates have officially submitted their bids for the FIFA presidency. Gianni Infantino, who has been in office for 11 years, is seeking a fourth consecutive term. Backed by UEFA, French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo wants to offer an alternative to Infantino’s leadership. He will face Japan’s Kohzo Tashima, honorary president of the Japan Football Association. The election will take place on March 18, 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Czechs protest en masse against 'concentration of power in one hand' and growing control over media
stories.description: As large demonstrations in the Czech Republic challenge Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's plans to change the funding model of public broadcasters, Mikuláš Minář, Chair of the Million Moments for Democracy movement, joins François Picard from Prague for Spotlight, warning that his country risks following Hungary and Slovakia in democratic backsliding. "We are really afraid that the Czech Republic is following the Orbánian Hungarian way, (Fico's) Slovakian way," he says.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: EU and UK set to sign deals on trade, energy, youth mobility at Brussels summit
stories.description: The UK and the EU are poised to agree new deals on trade, energy and youth mobility at a summit in Brussels on Friday, as part of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's bid to reset ties with the bloc. Burnham – who has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime – argues the deals will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
stories.subject: Business

stories.title: White House fires national cyber director over widespread outages
stories.description: The White House fired national cyber director Sean Cairncross on Thursday following a week of technology disruptions affecting US air travel, email services and national security systems. The departure comes as the Trump administration faces criticism over its response to the outages, which officials say were unrelated incidents.
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: PM Sánchez admits 'mistakes' in key debate ahead of Spain's election
stories.description: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledged shortcomings in his government on Thursday as he faced conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in the campaign's only televised debate. The November 29 election could leave the far-right Vox party in a position to enter government.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches one light-day milestone
stories.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years, hit a milestone distance of one light-day away from Earth on Wednesday. Already the most distant man-made object in the universe, the spacecraft is now about 26 billion kilometers (16 billion miles) away, according to the US space agency. That is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports.
stories.subject: Science

stories.title: Major anti-gang offensive in Haiti kills 34 suspected gang members
stories.description: Haitian security forces launched a major offensive on Thursday to retake Martissant, a strategic corridor linking Port-au-Prince with the country's western and southern regions that gangs have controlled for five years. Police said at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in clashes involving a private security task force.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
stories.description: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34% higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17%. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate
stories.description: French far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon opened the door to an alliance with France's Greens on Thursday after their presidential candidate Marine Tondelier said she was ready to "work on a coalition around" the veteran leftist. Tondelier's overture has further boosted Mélenchon's campaign for the Élysée Palace – and angered moderates on the centre-left.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Kenyan marathon champion banned for doping
stories.description: In tonight's edition, Kenyan athletics superstar and reigning marathon world champion Peres Jepchirchir is banned for three years for doping. Also, South African judges leave the courtroom behind and tour a repatriation centre before handing down judgment in 33 emergency asylum applications. And Ghana's presidency has a new jet, but critics of the ruling party are not on board.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill one, damage Dutch and Austrian embassies
stories.description: A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged a historic cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. Loud explosions erupted across the Ukraine capital throughout the day as the leaders of Russia, China and the United States held a historic meeting in China that put Russia's President Vladimir Putin in international spotlight. FRANCE 24's Laurent Berstecher reports.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: 'We're seeing in real time the effects that AI is going to have on cybersecurity', expert says
stories.description: FRANCE 24's Monte Francis speaks with Dr. R. David Edelman, Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, also former Director for Cybersecurity on the National Security Council under the Obama administration. He explains that the latest spate of network outages shows "in real time the effects that AI is going to have on cybersecurity" adding that "the one thing that's tying most of these outages together is that companies and institutions are racing to patch a system that's been identified as vulnerable, and they're patching what themselves are pretty creaky digital systems".
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: Kushner says Trump 'open' to extend NATO mutual defense-type clause to Ukraine
stories.description: US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday that President Donald Trump was open to extending to Ukraine a security guarantee similar to NATO's mutual defense clause, but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. The comments came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz qualified the summit between the presidents of the United States, Russia and China as a "photo op". FRANCE 24's international affairs commentator Douglas Herbert explains.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Macron urges Ukraine's allies to 'reopen the question' of NATO membership
stories.description: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called for Ukraine's allies to speed up the delivery of urgently needed air defence systems and urged them to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership after talks in Berlin aimed at reaffirming European support for Kyiv.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: A president among body bags: Photo ops spark outrage in Colombia
stories.description: Since taking office in August, Colombia's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella has regularly posted videos that show him walking among body bags supposedly holding the remains of rebel fighters – a communications strategy that has sparked widespread criticism.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Three of a kind? Xi hosts Trump and Putin as Ukraine war grinds on
stories.description: Gang of three or glorified photo op? Xi Jinping hosting Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Already, our Monday panel rejected attempts to paint the three-way meeting as a new Yalta, as in the 1945 sit-down on the Black Sea that defined the post-war security architecture of Europe.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting: Trump's recognition of China and Russia as 'peers of the US'
stories.description: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome Olivia Cheung. The trilateral meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit was significant despite the absence of concrete agreements, according to Cheung. “The significance is seen in the precedence of the United States seeing and giving recognition that China and Russia are peers of the United States,” she explained, adding that “the image of a G3 is very significant.”
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
stories.description: The Voyager 1 probe launched by NASA nearly a half century ago has reached a distance from Earth of one light day (more than 26 billion kilometres), the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from our planet. The space agency received a signal from the spacecraft Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent.
stories.subject: Science

stories.title: French media regulator says it will monitor top YouTubers for bias in election coverage
stories.description: Rules designed to safeguard media pluralism during elections campaigns will apply to France's most influential YouTubers in the run-up to next year's presidential contest, media regulator Arcom warned on Thursday, reflecting the growing influence of content creators whose audiences often outstrip those of traditional media companies.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
stories.description: Despite warm words between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen Thursday, the simmering trade war between Washington and Beijing still looks to be no closer to resolution.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Bangladesh: Hasina supporters vandalise ruling party office
stories.description: Hundreds of supporters of ousted Bangladesh premier Sheikh Hasina staged street protests on Thursday, as a wave of arson attacks escalated tensions ahead of her planned return from exile next month.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: US has 'unbalanced approach' on DR Congo deal, Rwanda's foreign minister says
stories.description: In an interview with FRANCE 24, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said the Trump administration had "an unbalanced approach" in implementing the DR Congo peace deal it brokered. He also said that the recent row over the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie's top job was "manufactured in Paris and Kinshasa". Finally, he defended a deal for Rwanda to host failed asylum seekers from five European countries.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: 🔴Anthropic soars more than 30% to $2 trillion valuation on first day of trading
stories.subject: World

stories.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
stories.description: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: Inside France's mental health crisis: Are the French all right?
stories.description: This week, we try to get inside the heads of French people, with a deep dive into mental health in France. For a nation that loves analysing its problems, its mental health figures make for sobering reading: nearly one in five French people are affected by a mental health issue.
stories.subject: Health

stories.title: ICJ ruling on Myanmar genocide: ‘Historic victory for Rohingya, landmark for international justice’
stories.description: Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Xi demonstrating China's 'global status', occupying 'central position' in relation to Trump & Putin
stories.description: Sharon Gaffney is pleased to welcome Rex Li, professor of international relations at King's College London. For Professor Li, the meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in China is less about "reaching concrete agreements and a common position." Rather, he argues, it is about demonstrating Xi's ability to bring the American and Russian leaders together to discuss major geopolitical issues. Li believes that Xi Jinping has the most to gain from the meeting, as it allows him to demonstrate China's global status and its role as a diplomatic convener. Putin may also benefit from the opportunity to meet the two leaders despite Russia's international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Gender pay gap: French women work "for free” from today
stories.description: Women in Europe are still paid less than men, with the gap falling from 15.1% in 2016 to 11.1% in 2024, according to Eurostat. In France, women symbolically start working for free from 10:51 am on Thursday, 19 November, and at the current pace equality would not be reached until 2062. Experts warn that AI could make things worse by eliminating administrative and legal jobs where many women work, while childbirth and short paternity leave continue to slow women’s careers.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: 'GTA VI': A masterpiece? Fans react to gaming's biggest release
stories.description: Critics are calling the new "Grand Theft Auto VI" a masterpiece. In this edition of arts24, we hear what fans make of one of the biggest video game releases in history. We also look at U2's new album and tour marking 50 years of the band, discover the French comic book that Pope Leo is reading and meet the women redefining Mexico's Mariachi tradition.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: The chocolate countdown: The art of the advent calendar
stories.description: The holiday season is almost upon us and with it come advent calendars. The annual physical countdown originated in 19th-century Germany as a Christian tradition to count down the days until Christmas. Eugénie Pont from the magazine Fou de Pâtisserie tells us more about what we can expect from the biggest chocolate makers in France.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Trump, Xi, Putin summit: What was it all about?
stories.description: Donald Trump has left China after a historic first meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Ukraine was discussed without Kyiv or European leaders in the room, which raised eyebrows, though Trump defended dialogue with rivals and Putin said the talks created conditions for future agreements. Xi warned major powers against conflict, and topics included reducing nuclear risks, reforming the UN and increasing energy flows.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Behind the UK's use of AI in asylum applications
stories.description: The UK is increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to manage its immigration system, from analysing migrants’ phones to processing asylum applications. But what happens when AI gets involved in deciding how an asylum seeker's story is understood? Stella Elgersma, journalist at InfoMigrants, explains how the UK Home Office is testing AI tools to process asylum applications, including a system that generates summaries of asylum interviews. With errors, limited human oversight and concerns over transparency, could AI put asylum seekers’ lives at risk?
stories.subject: Technology

stories.title: Haiti: Salvador’s Bukele publishes video of attack on gang leader’s house
stories.description: Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff Gwo Lwa. "My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières," Bukele wrote on X - referencing a 1803 battle critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Beaujolais Nouveau: A French tradition uncorked
stories.description: Every year on the third Thursday of November, France raises a glass to one of its most joyful traditions: Le Beaujolais Nouveau! That means that this Thursday, millions of bottles of the 2026 young red wine will be uncorked around the world, from Lyon to New York. Olivier Badoureaux, wine expert and director of the French trade organisation Inter Beaujolais, tells us what we should expect from this year's vintage.
stories.subject: Business

stories.title: France: Retirees march against 2027 budget cuts
stories.description: More than a thousand people marched in Paris on Thursday, called by a union alliance joined by student and high-school groups, to protest social and tax measures targeting retirees in the 2027 budgets. The government wants retirees to contribute about €5.4 billion, by freezing the indexation of pensions above €1,260 and reforming their 10% income tax allowance. Union leaders say the money should not come from retirees’ pockets, as FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago explains.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Chef Rachel Khoo: 'You don't need fancy kitchen gadgets to cook delicious food'
stories.description: One of the world's best-known chefs has spoken to FRANCE 24 about her new book that proves you certainly don't need fancy kitchen gadgets to cook delicious meals. The book "The Smallest Restaurant in Paris" tells her own story of starting out in a tiny Parisian flat cooking food just for two people at a time. That then led to a BBC series and a decade of writing and filming cooking stories. Rachel Khoo is now a judge on "The Great Australian Bake Off". She spoke to us in Perspective.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.description: In August 2017, after attacks by a Rohingya militia, Myanmar’s army launched a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state, with survivors describing mass killings, rapes and burned villages as hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh. The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ in 2019, and after a seven-year legal fight the court has ruled that Myanmar committed acts of genocide. Meanwhile some 1.2 million Rohingya remain in crowded camps, unable to return home.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: China summit ends with little new, Europe backs Ukraine in Berlin
stories.description: The leaders of China, the United States and Russia met in Shenzhen for a historic first, but the summit brought little new: non-binding statements on peace and no plan to meet regularly. In Berlin, Europeans gathered to show their support for Ukraine, a pointed answer to a summit where Europe had no seat, as FRANCE 24's Kethevane Gorjestani explains.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: In South Korea, women forced into prostitution on US military bases seek justice
stories.description: Tens of thousands of women were forced to work in South Korean state-sanctioned brothels used by American soldiers based in the country after the Korean War. They were raped, physically abused and forcibly confined. Now, after decades of silence, some of these women are speaking out.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: 'Their lives, their rights, their history': Not the end of accountability for the Rohingya people'
stories.description: Oliver Farry welcomes Sonya Sceats, Director and CEO of the British Institute of International and Comparative Law. The case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar before the ICJ, and the court ruling, both have great significance for the Rohingya people, the interpretation of the Genocide Convention and the possibility of future criminal proceedings. The case could also have important implications for South Africa's proceedings against Israel, where there are “many similarities between the two cases.”
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: 24-month matured Comté crowned world’s best cheese
stories.description: With its nutty flavour and smooth, supple texture, it was aged for two years in a former military fortress in eastern France. Comté, an unpasteurised cow’s milk cheese from the Jura Mountains, has beaten more than five thousand challengers to the top prize at the prestigious annual 'World Cheese Awards'. FRANCE 24's Daniel Whittington has the story.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Inside Limoges City Hall devastated by arson attack
stories.description: Work is underway to restore the city hall of Limoges, in central France, which was devastated by an arson attack during riots on October 17. More than €1.7 million has been raised through an online fundraising campaign in the wake of the disaster. Also on the show, the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI has finally been released, with gamers in Oceania among the first to get a taste of the latest instalment in the video game franchise.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: Crimea bridge strike: Fact-checking fake videos of damage after Ukraine's attack
stories.description: Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, but not all the dramatic footage circulating online is real. Multiple AI-generated videos falsely show the bridge collapsed with extensive damage. Some even used branding resembling a Ukrainian news agency to appear credible. While the bridge was indeed struck and damaged, the viral videos were fabricated using AI, as Vedika Bahl explains.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Bassirou Diomaye Faye excluded from Senegal's ruling party
stories.description: In tonight's edition, the political divorce between Senegal's president and the powerful former prime minister and mentor is official. Also, all of Nigeria's states have shown willingness for a push to create their own police forces. And in parts of the continent, conflict and a drop in funding have placed huge pressures on children's learning.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Reconstruction begins at Limoges City Hall after devastating fire
stories.description: It's been a month since the nationwide protests that degenerated in violence across France. The dramatic pictures of the historic City Hall in the French city of Limoges set on fire made headlines worldwide. To the relief of many, the reconstruction work on the building has now begun. Since the fire, donations have poured in and already about 80 percent of the necessary funding has been secured. FRANCE 24's Caitlin Brown reports.
stories.subject: World

stories.title: US Democrats nominate Jeffries to be first Black House speaker
stories.description: Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of becoming the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats elected him their leader Wednesday following a sweeping midterm election triumph. Jeffries faced no declared challenger, although opposition from some newly elected progressives had exposed divisions over how Democrats should wield their newfound power. FRANCE 24's Fraser Jackson reports from Washington.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Israeli army launches ground operation in Hamas-controlled area of Gaza
stories.description: The Israeli military said it had launched an operation on Wednesday in a Hamas-controlled area of central Gaza, where an AFP journalist saw Israeli tanks position themselves east of the Nuseirat refugee camp. The rare ground operation comes after inconclusive Israeli elections, with the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot trying to form a government without caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security. FRANCE 24's Daniel Whittington reports.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: 'Netanyahu's only 2 tickets are racism or starting a war: He stopped acting as a democratic player'
stories.description: François Picard is pleased to welcome Israeli writer and filmmaker Etgar Keret, author of "The Seven Good Years", joining us from Tel Aviv. Keret argues that Netanyahu is seeking to remain in power, at any cost, including delegitimizing Arab parties and prolonging conflict. “For him, it could be a never-ending war as long as he's in power. He has no incentive to stop it,” he warns. Keret also calls for Israelis to examine how the war in Gaza was conducted, arguing that “the media as a whole ignored the war.”
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Xi welcomes Trump: Does Nvidia scandal upend US-China AI race?
stories.description: You can strike Jensen Huang from the guest list but good luck steering dinner conversation away from the topic in Shenzhen. The co-founder of the AI computing leader was to accompany the US president to the APEC summit before he was undone by revelations of a dalliance with a Chinese national that happened to coincide with a Singapore client's backdoor skirting of sanctions on its powerful H200 chips.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Hegseth makes surprise trip to Venezuela, renews military cooperation
stories.description: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday, announcing a resumption of military cooperation with Venezuela and vowing to crack down on drug traffickers. The trip marks the highest-level US visit since the ouster of Nicolas Maduro in January, signalling a dramatic shift in relations between the two countries.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Why Ukraine keeps trying to bring down Russia's bridge to Crimea
stories.description: A Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Monday night brought down a stretch of the bridge linking the annexed Crimean Peninsula to Russia, potentially crippling a route long used by Moscow to move men and materiel into Crimea and the southern front. Here’s why Kyiv keeps testing its strength against an infrastructure project that has become synonymous with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 2014 seizure of the peninsula.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Beijing has supported Moscow but 'China understands that America is way more important than Russia'
stories.description: Following Xi Jinping's very friendly rare tarmac greeting for Donald Trump, Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies and Director of the Lau China Institute at King's College, London. Brown examines the complex relationship between the world's two largest economies, China's growing diplomatic influence and the competition over artificial intelligence.“China is the diplomatic center of the world,” says Brown, pointing to Beijing's ability to bring together leaders from Russia, the United States, Europe and elsewhere. He argues that China now has “extraordinary convening power" and significant influence over Russia.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: French ex-PM Philippe pledges to slash spending, hike retirement age as Elysée bid falters
stories.description: Former prime minister Édouard Philippe pledged on Wednesday to slash public spending, scrap France’s statutory 35-hour workweek and raise the retirement age to 65 from the current 62.9 years as he unveiled a slew of measures aimed a staving off economic "catastrophe" for France. An early frontrunner in next year's presidential election, Philippe is now trailing rivals in opinion polls and at risk of missing out on the second-round runoff.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: War in Ukraine: Is France in direct conflict with Russia?
stories.description: An investigation published by the French public radio channel RFI on November 17 revealed that a confidential mission by the French army known as "Volia" has been used for months to conceal the presence of French personnel in Ukraine. Russia was prompt to accuse France of direct involvement in the conflict. Is this true?
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Senate leadership challenge exposes divisions among Democrat
stories.description: As Democrats prepare to take control of the Senate, incumbent minority leader Chuck Schumer is facing an insurgent leadership bid from Senator Chris Van Hollen and disputes over party leadership are exposing divisions over what direction to take the Democratic party after their midterms sweep.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Russia’s new low-cost munitions pose a fresh threat to Ukraine
stories.description: Dan-T, Filin and Geran-5 might not mean anything to you, but in Ukraine, everyone is talking about these munitions. These new Russian weapons are small, fast and cheap – and a major threat, as they were specially designed to get around Ukrainian anti-aircraft defences and strike deep within the country.
stories.subject: Geopolitics

stories.title: Israel begins new military operation in Gaza
